title_clean: This Is the Wrong Time for Long-Term Options
summary: Rule: avoid long-dated (LEAPS-style) options until the Election Commission announces poll dates; the risk is a surprise outcome (2004: expected BJP win, ~30% fall; 2009: expected hung house, +20% circuit day) versus no surprise (2014, 2019: ~100-150 point moves). Counting day on a trading weekday allows stop-loss management; a holiday count creates unmanageable gaps and IV spikes.
lessons: Surprise, not the event, moves markets: expected outcomes produce 100-150 point moves; surprises produce 20-30% moves.
Avoid long-term options in election years until dates are announced.
If counting day falls on a trading weekday you can manage with stop-losses; on a holiday the gap risk is unmanageable.
IV rises for far expiries when uncertainty persists and collapses once the outcome is known.

title_clean: The Big Risks Behind Hedging - It's Not for Everybody
summary: Responds to critics of a 18-lakh single-day loss inside a 30-lakh profitable book. Core math: a 300-point hedge locks that loss when the market falls modestly; hedging cuts margin ~3x so traders size up 3x, restoring the same notional risk; annual hedge premium (~25,000 in the analogy) usually exceeds rare gap losses, so hedged and unhedged returns converge - hedges buy peace of mind. Also: capital handled matters more than ROI (FD-collateral 'infinite ROI' argument).
lessons: A hedge is insurance: it compensates but does not remove the loss (300-pt hedge = 300-pt locked loss).
Hedging shrinks margin ~3x; sizing up 3x quietly restores the original risk.
Annualized hedge cost typically exceeds the loss it prevents in normal years - hedges pay off only in tail events.
What matters is how much capital you can handle, not percentage ROI; a collateral-backed seller's ROI is 'infinite'.

strategies.risks: overnight gaps hurt both styles; unhedged size-ups restore tail risk

title_clean: The Flooding of Illegal PMS in India - Why No Hedge Funds!
summary: Explains why India lacks hedge funds despite the world's largest derivatives market: managing others' money outside license is illegal; SEBI AIF Category III is the legal route but the 2x notional-leverage cap makes option selling uneconomic (worked example: 0.2%/month), there is no company-rate taxation for hedge funds (43.7% slab), and Category III lacks tax pass-through (Cat I/II have it). Includes a long-short fund case study (SBI long cash + HDFC Bank short future through COVID) and the tax asymmetry that produced Rs 2.5L tax on Rs 50k profit.
lessons: The 2x notional-leverage cap makes option-selling strategies uneconomic inside AIF Cat-III.
F&O gains are business income (up to ~43% slab) while cash-market losses are capital losses - a long-short book can owe more tax than it earned.
Tax pass-through exists for AIF Cat I/II but not Cat III - the third structural reason India lacks hedge funds.
Long-short equity (long the stronger, short the weaker) profits in both directions if the spread thesis holds.
